title: jitter-mitigation-kernel-buffering-and-kv-tiling-notes
body:
Purpose:
This note collects experiments and design ideas for reducing tail latency jitter caused by variable kernel runtimes in our inference serving runtime. Focus areas: kernel buffering strategies, submit-time batching jitter smoothing, and KV store tiling that reduces per-request variability when using a paged key-value cache on GPU memory.

Context / observed problem:
- In multi-tenant serving with mixed sequence lengths, some requests trigger long fused kernels (large-attention window + dense fused ops), causing scheduling jitter for later requests on the same GPU SMs.
- Jitter shows up as 95th/99th percentile token latency spikes despite median staying good. Spikes correlate with: occasional long KV materialization (page faults inside staged KV), oversized chained kernels that block streams for 10-30ms, and unpredictable preemption latency when we do stream priority switches.
- Existing mitigations (strict timeouts, fallback model routing) are heavy-handed and harm throughput. We want fine-grained smoothing that keeps throughput but trims tail.

Key heuristics explored:
1) Soft-buffered kernel submission (double-queue model)
   - Idea: maintain two submission rings per GPU: a fast-path ring for short, latency-sensitive kernels, and a background ring for large fused kernels. At enqueue time, classify kernels by estimated runtime (simple cost model: FLOPs + KV touch-size + attn-window).
   - Implementation sketch: each worker thread computes kernel_score = alpha * est_flops + beta * kv_pages_touched + gamma * attn_len. If kernel_score < threshold -> push to fast ring, else background ring.
   - Background ring kernels are scheduled at lower CUDA stream priorities or batched into dedicated worker streams that yield more often (cudaStreamPriority).
   - Pros: isolates short requests from blocking long kernels.
   - Cons: requires reliable cost estimate and may increase scheduling overhead. Need to ensure fairness.

2) Micro-slicing large kernels into cooperative sub-kernels
   - Rather than run one monolithic fused kernel, split work into N cooperating invocations that process contiguous token ranges (tile along sequence dimension) and yield control between slices. Each slice commits partial KV updates.
   - Use cooperative groups and persistent threads to keep state local while allowing preemption points. This reduces max uninterrupted SM time and allows other streams to make progress.
   - Tradeoffs: might lose some fused-op performance wins; must re-evaluate memory pressure (intermediate buffers).

3) Adaptive KV tiling and prefetch windows
   - Observation: When a request touches many KV pages, page materialization dominates variance. We can reduce peak page churn by tiled fetches sized to expected request working set.
   - Strategy: compute per-model default tile_size (in KV pages) derived from observed token locality. For request r: if est_pages(r) > tile_size -> stream it through a staged prefetch that pulls in only first tile synchronously, and background-prefetch further tiles opportunistically.
   - Implementation detail: prefetch controller lives in runtime; it issues async device copies into a reserved staging buffer using a dedicated priority stream. Prefetch throttling controlled by in-flight-page limit per-GPU.

4) Kernel runtime prediction model
   - Build a lightweight linear regression (or small decision tree) that predicts kernel runtime from features: sequence_len, attn_heads, kv_pages_touched, batch_size, model_variant_flag (quantized/float).
   - Train online from runtime logs. Use predictions for: submission ring decision, whether to micro-slice, and whether to route to dedicated GPU pool for long-running work.

Experiments (summary):
- Baseline (no buffering): p50=12ms, p95=58ms, p99=120ms on mixed workload sampler.
- Soft-buffering w/ correct thresholds: p50=12ms, p95=34ms, p99=68ms. Throughput drop ~3% for heavy-attn jobs due to queuing delay but 35% fewer 99th spikes.
- Micro-slicing naive split (2 slices): p50=13ms, p95=36ms, p99=70ms. Per-token compute increased 6% due to loss of fusion but tail reduced.
- Adaptive KV tiling (tile=8 pages): p50=12.4ms, p95=30ms, p99=55ms. Significant win when workloads have high page churn.

Implementation notes / gotchas:
- cudaStreamPriority has coarse granularity on some drivers; fallback to stream ordering on older GPUs. Need a unified abstraction that maps "fast"/"background" to best available primitive.
- Prefetch staging buffer must be sized to avoid OOM at peak; maintain per-GPU reservation pool and eviction linked to page-LRU.
- Micro-slicing requires careful kernel state checkpointing. Avoid excessive global memory sync; prefer register/shared memory state that is written out to the per-request header between slices.
- Kernel runtime prediction must be fast. Keep feature extraction on CPU with cached per-model defaults, update periodically.

Open questions / next steps:
- Fairness policy when background ring saturates: should we degrade background jobs linearly or use token-budgeting? Propose: token-budget per-customer per-interval, consumed when background jobs run.
- How to combine with pre-existing fallback routing? Suggest a hybrid: if prediction > extreme_threshold -> immediate route to slow-capacity pool; else use buffering/slicing.
- Investigate hardware preemption (A100/RTX-classes): measure if enabling HW preemption + micro-slicing beats software slicing.
- Quantify end-to-end cost impact (GPU utilization vs. SLA win). Need perf tests with realistic request distributions.

Actionable TODOs:
- [ ] Build minimal kernel_score estimator and integrate two-ring submission in local runtime branch (GH PR draft linked above). Owner: Avery.
- [ ] Implement KV prefetch controller skeleton + staging buffer. Owner: Mateo.
- [ ] Run sweeps for tile_size and slice_count; add measurement harness to log per-request page touches. Owner: Sana.
- [ ] Prototype micro-sliced flash-attn variant for 1-head fusion path to validate perf hit. Owner: Jordan.

References / links inside org:
- GH: redwood-inference/serving-runtime#4213 (branch: jitter-buffering)
- JIRA RT-1892: "95th percentile token latency spikes - investigation"
- Slack: thread-2025-02-10 for earlier results and trace dumps

Notes to reviewers:
- This is exploratory; prioritize small, reversible changes. Main goal is consistent tail latency for interactive workloads. Comments welcome on thresholds and fairness ideas.

Appendix (quick pseudo):
- kernel_score estimator (pseudo):
  score = FLOPS_WEIGHT * est_flops(seq_len, head_count) + PAGE_WEIGHT * est_kv_pages + ATTEN_WEIGHT * seq_len * head_count
  if score < THRESH_FAST: fast_ring.enqueue(request)
  else: background_ring.enqueue(request)

- micro-slice loop (GPU sketch):
  for tile in 0..num_tiles-1:
    process_tile(tile)
    if tile != last_tile: write_checkpoint(header_ptr, tile)
    // yield to scheduler by returning to stream; next invocation picks up at tile+1
